Mon premier véritable contact avec ce su: My first real contact with this subject was the launch of the Mon enfant à défis! project, organized by the organization Entre-Parents de Montréal-Nord. An intimate gathering of people working in early childhood took place at the Le Carignan community activity centre. Social workers, representatives of the DPJ, parents, educators: all were there to discuss the issues surrounding the upbringing of children with special needs.
Les témoignages des mères monoparentales: The testimonies of single mothers seeking asylum are striking. They make you want to dig deeper into the issue, to better understand the reality of these women, of these families who face new obstacles because of their children's condition. Cultural differences, lack of resources, isolation, mental load: all of it is palpable in what people in the field say. That is what I wanted to bring to the forefront in this story.
« J’aimerais bien l’entendre parler, qu’: “I would really love to hear her talk, for her to call me mom, for her to explain her needs to me, her pain.”
Ces mots bouleversants résonnent encore: These heartbreaking words keep echoing long after you hear them. They belong to a single mother in Montréal-Nord whose youngest was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder at the age of three. What this mother describes is not just a personal story. It is a glimpse into a broader reality, shared by many families who have recently arrived in Quebec, particularly in a neighbourhood as multicultural as this one.
Montréal-Nord, dont près de la moitié de: Montréal-Nord, where nearly half the population has an immigrant background, is one of the most diverse boroughs in the city. According to a report by the Direction régionale de santé publique published in 2017, about 7% of asylum seekers in the metropolitan region already lived in the neighbourhood. Today, according to the Montréal-Nord community organizations consulted, that proportion has grown with the rise in immigration, particularly from the United States in recent years.
C’est dans ce contexte que l’organisme c: It is in this context that the community organization Entre-Parents steps in. For more than 40 years, it has supported families in vulnerable situations. During an interview at its offices, executive director Isabelle Alexandre gave us a portrait of the people her team works with every day.
« On suit actuellement plus de 600 famil: “We're currently following more than 600 families. Of those, 90% are asylum seekers. Most of them come from Haiti. We also see Latin American and North African families. They arrive with a lot of trauma, in the children as much as in the adults.”
Un enfant à besoins particuliers est un: A child with special needs is a child who, because of a developmental disorder, a disability or learning difficulties, requires specialized support at school, at home or in the community. Cases can include autism, language disorders, global developmental delay or attention deficit disorder.
Et pour les familles migrantes, ce besoi: And for migrant families, this need for support doesn't come alone. It adds to a series of already significant challenges: precarious immigration status, unfamiliarity with major institutions, language barriers, poverty, social isolation. What other families can get through with the help of their network or a well-oiled system becomes, for them, an extremely difficult journey.
« Ces enfants-là n’ont pas le même dépar: “These kids don't get the same start in life as the others. Some have crossed several countries, have been separated from their parents or have lived through trauma. That changes everything in their development. Some of the children we follow here were even born of rape, often because of the mother's migration journey. So the needs and the support are different,” says Isabelle Alexandre.
Malgré les besoins croissants, Montréal-: Despite growing needs, Montréal-Nord has no specialized services for these children with specific needs. Families often have to go to Laval or other boroughs to see specialists. For a single mother with no car, no stable job and sometimes no status, these steps are often complicated.
« Quand j’ai commencé à m’inquiéter pour: “When I started worrying about my daughter, she wasn't even a year old. She didn't respond to her name, she didn't babble. I started looking for answers. But it took a year to get a diagnosis,” says one of these mothers.
« Toute maman aimerait entendre la voix: “Every mom would love to hear her daughter's voice, talking, answering. She has still never responded to her name,” she adds.
Obtenir un diagnostic est une étape esse: Getting a diagnosis is an essential step toward accessing services. But once the diagnosis is made, the battle is far from over.
En tant que demandeuse d’asile, cette mè: As an asylum seeker, this mother had no access to subsidized daycare. When she arrived in the neighbourhood, she had to pay $40 a day for a spot in a non-subsidized daycare. A financial burden that forced her into a heartbreaking choice.
« À quoi ça sert ? Je me rappelle, j’ai: “What's the point? I remember, I had to stop working because I told myself: ‘Go to work and pay that kind of money? Better to stay home and look after her!’” the mom explains.
Et quand une place a enfin été disponibl: And when a spot finally opened up in a subsidized daycare, it was her daughter's autism diagnosis that became the problem.
« J’ai essayé dans deux garderies. On al: “I tried two daycares. They were going to accept my daughter, but because of her autism, they turned her down.”
Les obstacles ne s’arrêtent pas à la por: The obstacles don't stop at the daycare door, subsidized or not. In Montréal-Nord, the rates of reports to the Direction de la protection de la jeunesse (DPJ) are well above the Montréal average: 45.5% of cases involving children aged 0 to 4 concern a serious risk of neglect, and 38% are linked to a situation of domestic violence.
Mais ces chiffres, selon les intervenant: But according to the workers on the ground, these numbers don't tell the whole story.
« Quand les parents arrivent, il y a un: “When parents arrive, there's a double challenge. The first is cultural: the culture shock of arriving here forces them to figure out how things work. Then there's the issue of their child's developmental pace, which is different. The child isn't developing at the pace we were taught or that we might have read about in books,” explains Sandy Forge, a special education technician at Entre-Parents.
Elle-même mère de deux enfants autistes,: A mother of two autistic children herself, she is well aware of some families' reluctance to seek a diagnosis for their child.
« Je comprends les parents parce que j’é: “I understand the parents because I was in that reality: I didn't want my child to have a diagnosis because I was afraid of the label,” says the special education technician.
Cette méfiance face au système – qu’il s: This distrust of the system, whether the DPJ or the health or education networks, can be explained in part by a cultural gap between habits in the country of origin and Quebec's child-rearing norms.
« Lorsqu’on parle de facteurs de risque,: “When we talk about risk factors, it's a lot about neglect and abuse. That's what we call it. There are certain communities where, when it comes to raising the child… let's say the belt is part of discipline, or else there are threats of being sent back to the home country. They live in a system of fear, which means these aren't the practices here,” notes Isabelle Alexandre.
Différentes chercheuses en protection de: Various youth protection researchers highlight the complexity of the relationship between immigrant families and Quebec's DPJ system. They point to distrust and ethnocultural barriers on the part of youth protection staff, which leads to an overrepresentation of visible minorities in the system.
On évoque souvent des familles qui, sans: People often describe families who, without meaning to, find themselves up against major institutions like the health-care system or the DPJ, which don't use vocabulary suited to their frames of reference or their experiences. One of the many recommendations in the final report of the <l1>Laurent Commission</l1>, published in 2021, addresses this very issue.

Pour répondre à ces enjeux, Entre-Parent: To address these issues, Entre-Parents launched Mon enfant à défis!, the very first program of its kind in the Montréal-Nord neighbourhood. The initiative offers personalized support, group workshops and educational resources, but above all a place of listening and trust for these parents of children with special needs.
« Il faut comprendre que, si un enfant a: “You have to understand that if a child has a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder or an intellectual disability, it's a permanent diagnosis. It won't go away with time. It's important to be able to invest in the child's life as early as possible to help them progress,” Sandy Forge insists.
Grâce à ce projet, l’organisme espère ré: Through this project, the organization hopes to reduce reports to the DPJ, get more workers involved, and support 70 families and some 30 children within a year.
Malgré la fatigue, les sacrifices, les r: Despite the exhaustion, the sacrifices and the endless appointments, the mother we met has never stopped fighting for her daughter. When we ask her how she manages to hold on, she doesn't hesitate for a second.
« L’amour que j’ai pour elle, c’est quel: “The love I have for her is something I can't even explain. I don't know if it's because of her... well, I don't want to say ‘disability’… her problem… but I feel very attached to her,” the mom confides.
Les histoires de ces familles sont celle: The stories of these families are stories of resilience in the face of an often rigid system. They are also clear calls to reform our structures, to better train our workers and to adequately fund local community resources.
